recordings.text: Pattern: fork. One piece attacks several targets at once. Follow the shared attacker.
This offers the other side a way to set up a fork, attacking several targets with the same piece.
Missed resource: a fork. Another move offered a way to attack several targets with one piece.
The mechanism is a pin to the king. Leaving the line would expose the king, so that movement is not legal.
The other side has a chance to use a pin to the king. The pinned piece cannot leave that line and expose its king.
An alternative made use of a pin to the king. The pinned piece could not leave the line and expose its king.
Pattern: skewer. Moving the front piece exposes the piece behind it along the same line.
This offers the other side a route to a skewer. Moving the front piece could expose another piece behind it.
A stronger move offered a skewer. The front piece would move aside, exposing the piece behind it.
The idea is to capture a defender. Identify what it protects, then compare the position without it.
The other side has a chance to capture a defender. What it guards could then lose that protection.
Missed resource: capturing a defender. Another move offered a way to remove protection from what it guards.
The pattern is back-rank mate. The king's own pieces block its escape. Follow how the attack reaches it.
The other side has a route to back-rank mate. The king's own pieces form the barrier to escape.
A route to back-rank mate was available. This move passes up that finishing pattern.
The objective is promotion. Follow the pawn's route to the last rank, where it becomes a new piece.
This offers the other side a path to promotion. Follow the pawn that could reach the last rank.
Missed resource: promotion. A stronger move offered a route for a pawn to reach the last rank.
One piece moves aside, uncovering an attack from another. That is the discovered-attack pattern.
The other side has a discovered-attack opportunity. Moving one piece aside can uncover a threat from another.
Another move offered a discovered attack. Moving the blocker would uncover a threat from a different piece.
The idea combines two attacks at once. Track how the attacks work together.
This gives the other side a chance to combine two attacks at once. Both attacks need attention.
A stronger move offered two attacks at once. This move misses that combined threat.
Pattern: deflection. Draw a defender away from its task, then use the gap it leaves.
The other side has a chance to draw a defender away. Its original task could then go unattended.
Another move offered a deflection, drawing a defender away from its task. That opportunity was missed.
The idea is to capture an undefended piece. Locate the loose target before evaluating the capture.
An undefended capture was available in another line. This move misses the opportunity to take that loose piece.
The other side has a chance to capture an undefended piece. Check which piece could be left without protection.
Cause: the only effective defender moves away. Result: the other side can capture the piece it was guarding.
The previous move supplied the warning. This move leaves that attack unanswered, so the threatened piece can be captured.
The first capture is only part of the exchange. The recapture takes a more valuable piece. Count both sides.
A minor piece leaves its starting square and enters play. Development recorded.
The alternative would develop a minor piece from its starting square.
The rook now occupies an open file. There are no pawns of either color on that file.
The alternative would leave a rook on an open file, containing no pawns of either color.
The rook occupies a semi-open file. Friendly pawns are absent from it; enemy pawns remain.
The alternative would leave a rook on a semi-open file. Enemy pawns would remain there, but no friendly pawns.
The position now contains a passed pawn. No enemy pawn lies ahead on its file or the neighboring files.
The alternative would leave a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or either neighboring file.
The pawn was already passed. This move advances it. Compare its new position with the old one.
The alternative would advance the pawn that was already passed. Compare its destination on the board.
An isolated pawn remains in the position. Neither neighboring file contains a friendly pawn.
The alternative would leave an isolated pawn, with no friendly pawn on either neighboring file.
Support added. A piece that lacked a defender now has one.
The alternative would add support to a piece that was undefended before the move.
A piece is now undefended. That describes its support, not proof that it can be won.
The alternative would leave a piece undefended. That alone would not prove a winning capture.
The king gains a legal flight square. Compare the positions to see which change made it available.
The alternative would give the king a new legal flight square. Compare what would change around it.
The king castles. King and rook both change position.
The alternative was to castle. It would relocate the king and rook together.
This capture breaks the bishop pair. The side losing that bishop no longer has a bishop for each square color.
The alternative would capture a bishop and break the opposing bishop pair.
Doubled pawns remain in the position. Pawns of the same color occupy the same file.
The alternative would leave doubled pawns, with pawns of the same color sharing a file.
This move allows forced checkmate. Trace the attack to find where the defense fails.
A forced checkmate was available. This move loses that finish. Return to the position and locate it.
Sacrifice checked. Accepting the offered material does not refute it in the examined line.
This was the only playable move found. The other choices examined were losing.
This was the only move found that preserved the advantage. The other choices examined were losing.
A capture is available on the immediate reply. Check what the other side can take.
The strongest reply gives check. Responding to the threat to the king takes priority.
The engine prefers another move. Compare its replies on the board.
This move scores below the best option in the engine comparison. Inspect the reply for the difference.
A strong choice among the moves the engine examined.
Sound choice. It retains much of the position's value, though the engine prefers another move.
The human-move model rates this choice as natural. The engine finds a stronger move. Natural and best are different questions.
Unusual to the human-move model. Strong according to the engine. No contradiction.
The engine found a single playable defense. Model evidence suggests it was difficult to find. That resource was missed.
The human-move model and examined alternatives indicate a difficult move to find. Keep the pattern for future reference.
Defense found. The position remains playable. The human-move model and examined alternatives suggest this resource was hard to find.
Human-move estimate: natural. Engine comparison: best move. Both tests agree here.
The human-move model considers this natural. The engine considers it strong, but prefers a different move.
The recorded clock shows little time remaining before this move.
The clock records a quick decision with time still available.
The clock records substantial time spent on this decision.
Opening sequence matched. This move belongs to a recognized line.
Opening-book boundary reached. This is the first move beyond the recognized line.
Recovery confirmed. After the earlier setback, this move restores a playable position.
A playable position is restored. Errors by the other side helped make this recovery possible.
The opponent supplied an opportunity on the previous move. This move uses it.
The previous move supplied an opportunity. This response leaves it unused. Compare the stronger reply.
This issue has appeared earlier in the reviewed game. Compare the examples for a recurring warning sign.
Protection restored. The piece left unguarded earlier has support again.
The damage is cumulative. This move is part of several small concessions that worsened the position together.
The reviewed moves preserve the advantage through the recorded win. Follow that stretch to examine the conversion.
A matching issue appears in other saved games. Compare those examples with this one.
Checkmate confirmed. The king has no legal escape. Attack complete.
Checkmate confirmed. The king has no legal escape. Review the earlier defense for an intervention point.
Draw confirmed. The result is settled; earlier decisions remain available for review.
Position ready. Examine the board and select a move.
That attempt is not accepted. Recheck the position and try another move.
No analysis result was received. Return to the move to retry the request.
The saved engine analysis finds forced checkmate for the side that made this move.
After this move, the saved engine analysis gives the other side a forced checkmate.
Across the saved line, the moving side gains material relative to the starting position.
Across the saved line, the moving side loses material relative to the starting position.
Move accepted for this exercise. The displayed moves do not establish a clear tactical explanation.
Move not accepted for this exercise. A clear tactical reason is not established by the displayed moves.
Saved answer matched. Acceptance here is defined by the exercise's saved answers.
No saved answer matched. That does not prove a different legal move is bad chess.
Examine the move before proceeding to the next position.
Correct. Retain the reason as well as the move.
Practice recorded. The review schedule is unchanged.
Solved. Relearning status remains in place for this recall.
Starting position. The moves under examination begin here.
Next move displayed. Examine the changed position.
Check. The threat to the king requires an answer.
The king is no longer in check after this move.
Promotion completed. The pawn reaches the last rank and becomes a new piece.
Promotion completed, with check. The threat to the king must be answered.
Promotion and checkmate. The king has no legal escape.
The pawn promotes. The resulting position also removes the check against its king.
A piece is captured by this move.
Capture completed, with check. Both changes belong to this move.
The capture delivers checkmate. No legal escape remains for the king.
This capture ends the check against the moving side's king.
The pawn captures on the last rank and promotes. Capture and promotion completed.
The pawn captures and promotes on the last rank. The move also gives check.
Capture, promotion, checkmate. The king has no legal escape from the resulting position.
The pawn captures and promotes. That move also ends the check against its king.
The king castles, and the rook relocates. This move also gives check.
The king castles, and the rook relocates. Checkmate: the opposing king has no legal escape.
Follow the fork: one piece attacks several targets, then captures one. The example also shows a net material gain.
The indicated capture is illegal because of the pin to the king. Leaving the line would expose the king.
The attacked piece is pinned to its king. Its escape is restricted to moves that do not expose the king.
The defenders cannot recapture there: doing so would expose their king. The shown line yields a material gain.
The pinned piece cannot leave the line and expose its king. Follow the moves to see it captured.
The front piece moves off the line. The piece behind it is then captured along that same line.
The king leaves the line to escape check. The same attacker then captures the piece behind it in this example.
The only defender is captured. Later in the shown moves, the piece it guarded is captured as well.
The defender leaves its task. The piece it was guarding is then captured. Deflection demonstrated.
Moving the blocker opens an attack from another piece. That piece makes the capture along the new line.
The moving piece clears the line. Another piece now gives check through the opening.
Double check. Both pieces attack the king at the same time.
The moved piece attacks a target while another attacks along the opened line. That second piece captures its target in this example.
Follow the promotion. This example also establishes a net material gain for the promoting side.
The undefended piece is captured in this example. A net material gain for the capturing side is also established.
The opponent's preceding move released the attacker from a relative pin. The target stayed in place and is captured in the shown line.
The marked reply is legal for the other side. Play it to examine the next position.
Before selecting a move, check which friendly pieces can be captured without a useful recapture.
Inspect loose enemy pieces before selecting a quiet move.
Check forcing moves that attack two valuable targets at once. Track the shared attacker.
Before moving a pinned piece, identify what lies behind it: the king or a more valuable piece.
Look behind the first target. An attack may expose a valuable piece farther along the line.
Before exchanging a defender, identify what depends on its protection.
Inspect the lines that open when a blocking piece moves.
Search for a move that combines two threats. Include checks and newly opened lines.
Before moving a back-rank defender, inspect the king's escape squares.
Count the moves required for promotion. Check the forcing pawn advances.
Before moving a defender, identify every piece that will lose its protection.
Compare the value captured with the value lost to the recapture. Evaluate the whole exchange.
Check whether a forcing exchange draws a defender away from another target.
The saved answers set the exercise's acceptance rule. A different legal move is not automatically bad chess.
These moves demonstrate play against strong replies. Strong does not mean every reply is forced.
Material changes apply only to the shown line, measured from its starting position. The written notes specify the piece values.
The saved line establishes no simple tactical reason. Compare the replies directly; no positional cause has been inferred.
The saved answer policy governs this explanation. Its setting is recorded in the written notes.
The moves from the opening line under study are now displayed.
Match confirmed with the selected study material.
Select a move from the chosen study lines.
Any move from the selected opening lines is accepted here.
Recall a move from the selected study material.
That move is outside the selected opening lines. Choose another move.
That move is outside the selected lines. Retry is available. This saved attempt does not change the updated study's review schedule.
That move is outside the selected lines. Retry is available. This retired position's review schedule remains unchanged.
Mixed Due accepts moves from this line. Dedicated practice restricts answers to this line alone.
Scheduled recalls request moves for the selected side. Active studies share a single card when they share a position.
Reload the saved session before submitting another move.
The board is playing back the verified line.
Attempt recorded as revealed. The solution can be replayed below.
Solution completed after a retry. The record retains the earlier miss and the successful finish.
Full solution correct. No wrong moves recorded. Pattern resolved.
That move does not solve the puzzle. Earlier correct moves remain saved.
Move accepted. Find the next move required by the puzzle.
Position ready. Calculate before submitting a move.
The engine has not supplied enough information to explain this position.
Review paused. Resume it below, or move a piece to explore the position.
Select a move to review it, or move a piece to explore an alternative.
This is a recognized book move.
This move matches a known opening.
The move belongs to a recorded opening line.
The book sequence continues.
This is another book move.
This reply is book too.
Opening recognition continues.
This move stays within a known opening.
Another opening move is recognized.
This move also matches the opening record.
Opening record still matched.
Issue: forced mate for the opponent. The human model finds this move natural.
Available finish: forced checkmate. This move lets it go. Human-model reading: natural.
Immediate reply: the opponent can capture. The human model finds this choice natural.
Engine comparison: this move scores below the best option. Human-model signal: natural choice. A plausible move can still be weaker.
Issue: a fork is available to the opponent. One piece could attack several targets. The human model finds this choice natural; the tactical cost is still there.
Issue: the opponent has a skewer opportunity. Moving the front piece could expose the piece behind it. Natural to the human model. Costly on the board.
The difficult defensive resource was found. This was the only playable move among those searched; the other examined choices were losing.
Only this move stayed playable among those searched. The other examined choices were losing. Human-model evidence suggests a difficult find.
This difficult resource retained the advantage. It was the only move found to do so; the other examined choices were losing.
Advantage retained by this searched move only. The other examined choices were losing. Human-model evidence suggests a difficult find.
Fork resource found. The same piece can attack several targets. The human model finds the choice unusual; the engine finds it strong.
Resource: a fork. One piece can threaten several targets at once. The engine ranks this move best; the human model and searched alternatives suggest it was difficult to find.
Pin resource found. A piece pinned to its king cannot leave the line and expose it. The human model calls the choice unusual; the engine supports its strength.
Mechanism: a pin to the king. The pinned piece cannot leave that line and expose its king. This is the engine's best move; model evidence and searched alternatives indicate a difficult find.
Cause: the only effective defender moves away. Result: the opponent can capture the piece it guarded. The human model finds this choice natural.
The only effective defender moves away, leaving the guarded piece available for capture. The only playable defense found was missed. Human-model evidence suggests a difficult resource.
Warning: the opponent's previous move enabled the threat. This move leaves it unanswered, allowing the threatened piece to be captured. Natural to the human model; costly on the board.
Threat unanswered. The opponent can capture the piece left under threat. The only playable defense found was missed. Human-model evidence suggests it was difficult to find.
Exchange: the opponent can recapture a more valuable piece. The human model finds the initial capture natural. Count both sides.
The first capture invites a recapture of a more valuable piece. The only playable defense found was missed. Human-model evidence suggests a difficult find. Both halves of the exchange count.
Fork resource found. One piece can attack several targets. The human model considers the choice natural; the engine ranks it best. One attacker, several problems for the other side.
Resource: a fork, with several targets for the same piece. Natural to the human model and strong according to the engine. A different move still gets the engine's first choice.
Issue: the opponent can work toward a fork, attacking several targets with one piece. The search found only one playable defense. It was missed; human-model evidence suggests a difficult find.
Missed resource: a fork. Another move offered several targets for one attacker. The human model finds the played choice natural, but it passes up that opportunity.
Missed resource: a fork. One piece could attack several targets. That alternative was the only playable move found by the search; the human model indicates a difficult defense to find.
Resource: a pin to the king. Leaving that line would expose the king, so the pinned piece cannot do it. Natural to the human model. Best in the engine comparison.
Pin resource found. A piece pinned to its king has a legal restriction: it cannot expose the king. The model finds the choice natural; the engine finds it strong, while preferring another move.
Issue: a pin to the king is available to the opponent. A pinned piece cannot leave that line and expose its king. The human model finds this choice natural, despite the tactical problem.
Issue: the opponent has a chance to use a pin to the king. The only playable defense found by the search was missed. Human-model evidence suggests it was difficult to find.
Missed resource: a pin to the king. Another move could exploit the pinned piece's inability to expose its king. The played choice is natural to the human model, but loses that opportunity.
Missed defense: a resource using a pin to the king. The pinned piece could not legally expose its king. Only that alternative stayed playable in the search; model evidence suggests a hard find.
Resource: a skewer. Moving the front piece can expose the piece behind it along the same line. The engine ranks this move best; model evidence and searched alternatives indicate a difficult find.
Skewer resource found. The front piece can move aside and expose a target behind it. Unusual to the human model, strong according to the engine.
Resource: a skewer. The threat reaches the rear piece when the front piece leaves the line. The human model finds the choice natural; the engine ranks it best.
Skewer resource found: a front piece can move away and expose a rear target. The model finds this natural; the engine calls it strong, but puts another move first.
This choice offers the opponent a skewer. Moving the front piece could expose the rear piece. The only playable alternative found was difficult to spot.
Missed resource: a skewer. Moving the front piece could expose the target behind it. The human model finds the played choice natural; the stronger alternative offered that line attack.
Missed defense: a skewer resource. Moving the front piece could expose the one behind it. This was the only playable alternative found in the search; human-model evidence indicates a difficult find.
Resource: capture the defender. Its removal can leave what it guards without that protection. The engine ranks this move best; the human model and searched alternatives suggest a difficult find.
Target: a defender. Capturing it can remove the protection it supplies. The human model finds this choice unusual; the engine finds it strong.
Resource: removing a defender by capture. What it protects could then lose that support. The human model considers this choice natural, and the engine ranks it best.
A defender is the tactical target. Capture it, and the protection it supplies can disappear. Natural to the human model; strong according to the engine, which still prefers another move.
Issue: the opponent has a chance to capture a defender. Its removal could take away needed protection. The human model finds this choice natural; that lost protection is the tactical cost.

Issue: the opponent can target a defender for capture. What it guards could lose protection. Only one alternative stayed playable in the search. It was missed; model evidence suggests a difficult find.
Missed resource: capturing a defender. Another move could remove the protection that piece supplies. The human model favors the played choice, but the useful target was the defender.
Missed defense: a resource that captures a defender and removes its support. It was the only playable move found by the search. Human-model evidence suggests this was a difficult resource to find.
Resource: a route to back-rank mate. The pattern traps the king behind its own pieces. The engine ranks this move best; the human model and searched alternatives indicate a difficult find.
Back-rank mating route found. In this pattern, the king's own pieces form the barrier to escape. The human model finds the move unusual; the engine finds it strong.
Resource: back-rank mate. The pattern uses the king's own pieces to block escape. The human model sees a natural choice, and the engine ranks it best.
Back-rank mating route found. The pattern uses the king's own pieces to block escape. Natural to the human model and strong according to the engine; another move remains its first choice.
Objective: promotion. A pawn has a route toward the last rank and a new piece. The engine ranks this move best; model evidence and searched alternatives suggest it was hard to find.
Promotion route found. The pawn's destination is the last rank, where it can become a new piece. Unusual to the human model. Strong according to the engine.
Objective: bring a pawn to the last rank and promote. This move offers a route toward it. The human model calls the choice natural; the engine ranks it best.
Promotion is the tactical objective: a pawn reaching the last rank. The human model finds this choice natural, and the engine finds it strong. Its preferred move is still a different one.
Issue: an opposing pawn has a promotion opportunity. Reaching the last rank would turn it into a new piece. The human model finds this choice natural; the promotion threat remains.

Issue: a promotion route is available to the opponent. The pawn could reach the last rank. Only one searched alternative kept the position playable; model evidence suggests that missed defense was difficult to find.
Missed resource: promotion. Another move offered a pawn a route to the last rank. The human model finds the played choice natural, but that choice passes up the opportunity.
Missed defense: a resource built around promotion. A pawn could work toward the last rank. The search found no other playable move; human-model evidence suggests a difficult find.
Resource: a discovered attack. Moving one piece aside can reveal an attack from another. The engine ranks this move best; the human model and searched alternatives suggest it was difficult to find.
Discovered-attack resource found. One piece can move aside and uncover the attacker behind it. Unusual to the human model, strong according to the engine.
Resource: a discovered attack. Moving the blocker can open another piece's line of attack. Natural to the human model. Best in the engine comparison. The blocker can do useful work by leaving.
Discovered-attack resource found: one piece can move aside to reveal another attacker. The model finds this choice natural; the engine finds it strong, with a different move ranked first.
Issue: the opponent has a discovered attack available. Moving one piece aside could uncover a threat from another. The human model finds the choice natural, despite that hidden threat.

Issue: a discovered-attack opportunity for the opponent. One piece could move aside and reveal another threat. The sole playable defense found by the search was missed; model evidence suggests a difficult find.
Missed resource: a discovered attack. Another move could shift a blocker and reveal a different attacker. The human model favors the played choice; it still leaves this resource unused.

Missed defense: a discovered-attack resource. One piece could move aside to uncover another's threat. Only that alternative stayed playable in the search. Human-model evidence indicates a difficult find.
Resource: a double attack. Two threats can arrive together and demand attention at once. The engine ranks this move best; the human model and searched alternatives suggest a difficult find.
Double-attack resource found. The position offers a way to create two threats at once. Unusual to the human model. Strong according to the engine.
Resource: a double attack, bringing two threats into play together. The human model finds this choice natural; the engine ranks it best.

Double-attack resource found. Two attacks could demand attention at the same time. The human model finds this natural, and the engine finds it strong. A different move remains the engine's first choice.

Issue: the opponent can work toward two attacks at once. That is the double-attack opportunity this move permits. The human model finds the choice natural; both potential threats still need an answer.

Issue: a double-attack opportunity for the opponent. Two threats could arrive together. The only playable defense found by the search was missed; human-model evidence indicates a difficult resource to find.
Missed resource: two attacks at once. Another move offered that double threat. The human model considers the played choice natural, but it passes up the combined pressure.
Missed defense: a double-attack resource. Two threats could be created at once. It was the only playable alternative found by the search; human-model evidence suggests it was hard to find.
Resource: deflection. A defender can be drawn away from its task, leaving a gap. The engine ranks this move best; model evidence and searched alternatives suggest a difficult find.
Deflection resource found. A defender can be drawn away from the job it was doing. The human model finds the choice unusual; the engine finds it strong. The abandoned task is the target.
Resource: deflection. Draw a defender away, and its original task can go unattended. Natural to the human model; best in the engine comparison. The defender cannot do its old job from everywhere.
Deflection resource found. A defender could be pulled away from what it protects. The human model finds this choice natural, and the engine finds it strong while preferring a different move.
Issue: the opponent has a deflection opportunity. A defender could be drawn away from what it protects. The human model finds this choice natural; the unattended task is the tactical cost.
Issue: the opponent can work toward drawing a defender away from its task. The only playable defense found by the search was missed. Human-model evidence suggests that resource was difficult to find.
Missed resource: deflection. Another move could draw a defender away from its protective task. The human model favors the played choice, but the chance to exploit that task was lost.
Missed defense: a deflection resource. A defender could be drawn away from what it guards. Only that alternative stayed playable in the search; human-model evidence suggests it was difficult to find.

Resource: capturing an undefended piece. A loose target could be taken without a defender to protect it. The engine ranks this move best; model evidence and searched alternatives indicate a difficult find.
Undefended-capture resource found. The target could be taken without a piece guarding it. Unusual to the human model, strong according to the engine.
Resource: an undefended capture. A loose piece could be taken. The human model finds the choice natural, and the engine ranks it best.
Undefended-capture resource found. The tactical target is a piece without protection. Natural to the human model and strong according to the engine; the engine still prefers another move.
Missed resource: an undefended capture. A stronger choice offered a way to take the loose piece. The human model finds the played move natural; the opportunity remains unused.

Missed defense: an undefended-capture resource. The loose piece could be taken. That alternative was the only playable move found by the search; human-model evidence suggests it was difficult to find.
Issue: the opponent has an undefended-capture opportunity. A piece could be taken without protection. The human model finds this choice natural; a loose target can still be expensive.
Issue: a loose piece could be captured by the opponent. The search found only one alternative that kept the position playable. It was missed; human-model evidence suggests a difficult defensive find.
A minor piece develops from its starting square. The human-move model and checked alternatives suggest this move was difficult to find.
Development recorded. A minor piece leaves its starting square. Human-model signal: unusual. Engine assessment: strong.
This develops a minor piece from its starting square. The human-move model considers the choice natural, and the engine ranks this exact move best.
A minor piece develops from its original square. Natural according to the human-move model; strong according to the engine, which still prefers a different move.
A rook stands on a file with no pawns of either color. The human-move model and examined alternatives suggest this move was difficult to find.
Rook on an open file. No pawns of either color occupy it. The human model finds the choice unusual; the engine finds it strong.
The rook is on an open file, free of pawns of either color. This move is also natural in the human-move model and best in the engine comparison.
This leaves a rook on a pawn-free file. The human-move model calls the choice natural. Engine result: strong, while preferring a different move.
Rook on a semi-open file. Enemy pawns present; friendly pawns absent. Human-model evidence and the examined alternatives suggest a difficult find.
The rook's file contains enemy pawns and no friendly pawns. This semi-open-file position follows a move the human-move model considers unusual and the engine considers strong.
Semi-open file occupied. Enemy pawns remain on the rook's file; friendly pawns do not. The move is natural to the human model and best in the engine search.
Semi-open file: enemy pawns remain on the rook's file, with no friendly pawns. The played move is natural to the human-move model and strong to the engine, which prefers an alternative.
The move leaves a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or neighboring files. The human-move model and examined alternatives suggest this was a hard move to find.
Passed pawn present. No enemy pawn lies ahead on its file or the neighboring files. The human model finds the choice unusual. The engine finds it strong.
The position contains a passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead on its file or either neighboring file. Move assessment: natural to the human model, best in the engine search.
A passed pawn is left with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or neighboring files. The human-move model rates the move natural; the engine finds it strong but prefers another move.
The pawn was already passed. This move advances it. Human-model evidence and the examined alternatives suggest a difficult find.
Passed pawn advanced. It was already passed before this move. The human model marks the choice unusual; the engine judges it strong.
Passed pawn advanced. Its passed status was already established. The choice is natural to the human model and ranks first in the engine search.
The pawn was passed before the move. Now it advances. The human model considers the choice natural; the engine finds it strong but prefers another move.
The move leaves an isolated pawn, without friendly pawns on neighboring files. The human-move model and examined alternatives suggest this was a difficult move to find.
Isolated pawn present. Neither neighboring file contains a friendly pawn. The move is unusual to the human model and strong according to the engine.
An isolated pawn is present: no friendly pawn on either neighboring file. The human model considers the move natural. The engine selects it as best.
An isolated pawn is left without friendly pawns on neighboring files. The move is natural in the human-move model and strong by the engine's assessment, though the engine prefers another.
Support added. Previously undefended; now guarded. Human-model evidence and the examined alternatives suggest the move was difficult to find.
Support added. A previously undefended piece gains a defender. The human model finds the choice unusual; the engine rates it strong.
Support added to a piece that lacked a defender. The human model sees a natural choice. The engine confirms this as its best move.
Before the move: no defender. After it: support added. The choice is natural to the human model and strong to the engine, though another move ranks best.
Support removed. Missing support alone does not prove a winning capture. Human-model evidence and the examined alternatives suggest a difficult find.
A piece loses its defender. That proves a support change, not a winning capture. The human model finds this move unusual; the engine rates it strong.
A piece is left without a defender. That alone does not prove a winning capture. The move is natural to the human model and first in the engine ranking.
Undefended piece recorded. Missing support alone does not prove material loss. The human model considers the move natural; the engine finds it strong but prefers another move.
A new legal flight square is available to the king. Human-model evidence and the checked alternatives suggest a difficult find.
King mobility changed: a new legal flight square is available. The human model finds the move unusual; the engine finds it strong.
The king gains a legal flight square that was previously unavailable. The move is natural to the human model and best in the engine comparison.
A legal flight square opens for the king. The human-move model considers the move natural; the engine rates it strong but prefers another choice.
The king castles; king and rook have both moved. The human-move model and checked alternatives suggest difficulty finding this move in this position.
